title: Talking about Dark Retreat, with Andrew Holecek

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, Vajrayana, jhanas, the darkness, predictive processing, psychedelics, nonduality, consciousness hacking, and much, much more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm speaking with Andrew Holecek. Andrew Holecek is an interdisciplinary scholar-practitioner in Tibetan Buddhism and other non-dual wisdom traditions. He's the resident contemplative scholar at the Institute for Advanced Consciousness Studies, and a research consultant for the Cognitive Neuroscience Program at Northwestern University. His work involves studies on dream yoga and the practice of dark retreat, and he is the author of nine books. And now, without further ado, I give you the episode that I call Talking About Dark Retreat with Andrew Holecek.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Andrew, welcome back to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Hey, Michael. It's always so much fun to hang with you. Appreciate it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Right? We have a great time talking. In our last non-recorded conversation, you were super jazzed about dark retreat and stuff about the dark. So, I'm just ready. I'm like, Andrew, tell me about darkness and dark retreat and dark matter stuff.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Yeah. Oh, my gosh. Yeah. I was pretty psyched about it. Michael, I've been doing this particular practice, which we can unfold, for nearly three decades. I started studying it in 1996 with my main teacher in the school of Tibetan Buddhism at that time, Khenpo Tsultrim Gyamtso Rinpoche. And so I've almost literally been a kind of closet meditator, practicing this somewhat in secrecy, and I can share a little bit about why this practice has been kept secret. I go in annually, and a year and a half ago I went in, and I can tell you, like, you know, why and what you do and all that kind of stuff. There's too much to talk about. But this was a particularly transformative retreat, because at the end of it, this book just burst into my mind. I mean, literally, I felt like a little Mozart symphony or whatever. It just, boom, book. And I came out just wide open with this tremendous energy. And so I literally put this pen to paper as quickly as I could put words to paper, wrote this thing. On one level, it was the easiest book I ever wrote, because it really started the way I didn't write it. It just kind of just channeled through me. It's a tricky word these days. And I can say a little bit more later about how it turned out to be one of the most difficult books I've written, just because of the nuance, the depth, and the things that are being revealed. But since then, Michael, oh, my gosh, it's like the world has unfolded. We have one official scientific study underway. So I'm working with actually several different teams of scientists to officially study it. We're getting funding for even more research along these lines. I can say, and then I'll pause to come up, because there's so many directions to take this. I've done a lot of practice in my life, three-year retreat, probably 30,000 hours plus. And I can very safely say, at least for me, and this practice is not for everybody, but at least for me, this is hands down the most transformative thing I've ever done. So, I'll pause for a second, because there's just so many directions we can take this.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, and two things. What is it, number one? And number two, why is it or was it so secret?

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Yeah, great question. So, just to put a little historical context here, which I think is important, it goes back into the wisdom traditions. I mean, you can almost imagine, can't you, Michael, that even in the early pre-indigenous days, cave dwellers and whatnot were involved with dark practice. But the pre-Socratics did it. Peter Kingsley is a wonderful scholar. You may know his work, and his magisterial book, In the Dark Places of Wisdom, talks about Parmenides and the other pre-Socratics doing this practice. Iamblichus, who's a Neoplatonist, talks about dark retreat. You'll find it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Iamblichus talks about yidam practice, too. It's interesting.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Exactly. Oh, my gosh. Yeah, the Hellenic Tantra book. He talks about theurgy and yidam practice.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That book blew me away, by the way.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: So, lots to say on that front as well. But you'll find it in indigenous shamanic traditions, the Kogi tribe out of Colombia. They have an incredibly challenging way of training their shamans through extensive practice. But for me, the biggest formative context here comes from the Tibetan Buddhist and Bön traditions. And there are three strands here. In Tibetan Buddhism proper, and I studied all three of these, the Kalachakra strand, which is really, really beautiful, that's augmented by the Nyingma strand. So these are geek speak for some of the technical traditions and schools of Tibetan Buddhism proper. So there are four schools of Tibetan Buddhism: Kagyu, Nyingma, Sakya, Gelug. In the Kagyu, Sakya, Gelug, they work with the Kalachakra, the Wheel of Time Tantra. It's an unbelievably profound tantra. And since you brought the topic up, in the apex of that tantra, what are called the six limbs or the six yogas of the completion stage — it gets a little technical here, but these work with dark retreat, sensory deprivation. And I can return to there, how that strand is different from the Nyingma approach. But I've had education and training in both of those. And then also the Bön, the pre-existing indigenous tradition of Tibet, the Bön tradition also has a very rigorous exploration of the nocturnal mind. So that's the historical kind of framing. The reason it's secret and the reason I haven't talked about it is, traditionally in Tibet people would go in for 49 days, which is, like, that's a long time. It's arguably — and I would agree with this argument — the penultimate preparation for death. You really do enter the death space. And so what would happen, Michael, is that ill-prepared or unsupported practitioners, instead of attaining enlightenment, they'd attain madness. They'd attain insanity. And we can talk a little bit about why. Like, why is that the case? And so the practice fell out of favor. And then it slowly come back into the West through the work of one of my dear — I actually can call him a friend and also teacher — Tenzin Wangyal Rinpoche. He works with his community. Tulku Sangak Rinpoche works with his community. Well, they fly under the radar a little bit. And so when I started doing this with my training with Khenpo Rinpoche, I remember very clearly I went to another teacher, not him. Actually, it was Shakyamuni Rinpoche at the time. And I started to share some of my experiences in dark. This is almost two decades ago. And Rinpoche knew that at that point I was starting to write and publish and teach. And he's wonderful. I love him. And he said at the end of my first visit with him, I'm paraphrasing a little bit, he said, you know, Andrew, you can write, you know, talk about anything, but please keep this practice to yourself. And I had like zero issue with that, Michael. I said, oh, yeah, absolutely. I'm not going to say anything about it. And so, like, why now? And that just sent the first of two books off to my publisher. So, why now? Well, a number of reasons for why now. It's out there in the milieu, or it's getting out there. Superstars like Aaron Rodgers, you may know, went into dark retreat. And this is one of the more mind-blowing podcasts I've ever come across. There's actually a clip of Tucker Carlson in conversation with Aaron Rodgers. So Aaron put it on the map in a certain way. And then since then, Rudy Gobert, Dwight Howard — these are NBA superstars, athletes, scholars, artists and like are going in. They're starting to post on it. They're starting to write on it. And some of the stuff that's coming out there is not all that great because, for instance, here's one extreme example. There in some sporting magazines over the last couple of years, and I can reference these, there are literally articles of the following, that they talk about darkness as the next extreme meditation, the next extreme sport. You know, there's one article about this gentleman who conquered K2, second largest peak in the world. And then it says, well, his next conquest will be seven days on the dark. Oh, man, kidding me. And so this is like the absolute worst way to go into this, because if you go in with a somewhat white-knuckling machismo, bruised-to-the-finish-line kind of thing, the darkness will crush you and you can hurt yourself. We can have a nice little riff, if you'd like. In fact, a number of the scientists I'm working with do a lot of studies with psychedelics, and the relationship, Michael, between dark retreat and psychedelics is uncanny. And so just like with psychedelics, set and setting are important. You can absolutely, positively overdose. In this case, you're overdosing on yourself. And so dosages are really important. Using that metaphor, it's not that I have the AAA gold standard. Of course, I don't. But I've done this for a really long time. There's a lot of ways to do it right, but there are even more ways, in my estimation, of doing it wrong. And so I felt compelled to come out and speak about it. And I think I can do so — in fact, I've had the blessing of other Tibetan masters at this point — for the following reason. This is my languaging. You won't find this in the tradition, but we can talk about this difference as well. There's two ways to look at dark practice. One is the more traditional kind of tantric way, which is where you go in for, you know, up to these 49 days and you work with very specific sets of practices to cultivate very specific types of experiences. I'm not touching that baby. I'm not going there, at least in the public arena, because that kind of prescription-strength practice really needs to be done with a direct supervision of a physician, so to speak, right? It has to really be done properly, or you can and you will hurt yourself. The type that I'm writing about, my languaging is a more over-the-counter, exoteric sutra level, which is basically — and this is where we can riff — it's just like going into the dark anywhere from a couple hours to a couple days. For me, I'm doing it from a couple hours to the five-day limit, just to see what happens when you're in such a unique environment, what happens with such intense sensory deprivation. And so there's a tremendous amount of material coming out about amazing healing, creativity, insights. I mean, just like one remarkable benefit after the other. And there are only a few retreat centers in the country. I connected to almost all of them. And so I'm constantly talking to people. I've talked to or heard reports at this point, Michael, from literally hundreds of practitioners doing like three days, four days on the dark. And then I have my little group of friends who've done, you know, more of the levels that I work at. And Michael, the benefits are just insane. The ROI, the return on investment, is crazy. So what happens in a dark practice, Michael, is you go into a specially prepared cave or cabin where light is 100% removed. You're literally bolted in, so to speak. And it's not just light that's radically curtailed, but also sound. So it really is as close as you can get to a complete sensory deprivation situation. Food is delivered. Depending on where you go, there's a number of ways to manage that. The practical necessities actually are among the easier things that one was going to be having to deal with. But it is a unique and, from the outside, just downright bizarre kind of thing to do. It's like entering into a kind of a voluntary tomb or a sensory straitjacket. But it is precisely this level of restraint, curtailment, that brings about such radical transformation. So in terms of the practicalities behind it, that part is relatively straightforward. It's not easy, but it's relatively straightforward. You can start the practice at home, using eye masks. There's different types of, like the Manta, M-A-N-T-A, eye mask, which is the one I recommend, completely blocks out the light. That gets you started. You can block off a space in your room, closet, basement, which is actually what I have. I have a part of my basement closed off, and I'll do one or two days there. But in my experience, if I go beyond the two-day mark, I really need to go to a retreat center, because I can hear distant sounds. I can hear planes, even though I'm as far down my basement as I can get. And so something about the retreat aspect, the complete sensory deprivation, is key. Now, in terms of what one does there, in addition to the esoteric tantric stuff, which we can leave to the side, honestly, Michael, and this is where it becomes so remarkable, the absolute most important thing you can do is absolutely nothing. It's just sit in complete silence and stillness, what the Buddhists sometimes call non-distracted non-meditation, or Hindus sometimes talk about as the way of anupaya, the path of no path. And you literally just do nothing. And we can say more about that, because this is where all the healing comes from. This is where all the restoration, the creativity, because what I've discovered is this type of curtailment of the externally oriented senses, you know, almost hurls you into the depths of the interiority of your being. And so in the Tibetan tradition, it's actually referred to as a wrathful, or I should say forceful, method of liberation. It's forceful because darkness is non-negotiable and uncompromising. You know, you can't really move in the normal ways, you certainly can't perceive in normal ways, and it radically, you say, frustrates or interrupts our usual habitual patterns and tendencies. And it forces you into what we're languaging in our scientific studies — invites you, and then eventually forces you into what we're calling the reduction base of innate wholeness, which is fundamentally to talk about the ground or the basis of the non-dual mind. And so I'll pause for a second there, because this is where it gets super interesting, in terms of the actual journey of the spelunker, you know, the nocturnal, the explorer of the dark mind, so to speak. I can say a little bit more about my experience there, why I found it so compelling, why it's so revelatory, why it just has so many insanely positive outcomes. But at the same time, and let me say this — I guess this is really important as a disclaimer — this practice is definitely not for everybody. In fact, one of the main reasons I wrote the book was just as much to keep people out as it was to invite people in. Because as I mentioned earlier, if you go in with kind of an overachieving type A mindset, if you go in without proper preparation, proper set and setting, you may find yourself really, really struggling. And then what's the point? So it's important to understand that there are a host of contraindications here. We can get into some of those psychological, psychiatric contraindications. There are some physical contraindications. And so again, like with psychedelics, the holding environment, the set and setting, are really important.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, what's it like for, just say, an average non-insane person to do this for, like, let's say, what's a minimum dose of this? Like, maybe eight hours or something?

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: This is a really excellent question. So, minimum — again, the dosage thing is a really interesting one, because, you know, the darkness is really not about darkness, right, Michael? The darkness is about you. Darkness just provides an incredible metaphysical mirror where you can explore the nature of yourself without distraction, in the most intense environment possible. So it's not about darkness, it's about you. It's about discovering who you are. And so with that in mind, the way I teach it, I play on the classic Tibetan 49-day model. And then I'm definitely not saying you go in for 49 days. Don't do that. What I do is I go, okay, let's — in fact, let's do it together. You and our listeners, we're going to do our first dark retreat together. Okay. For the next 4.9 seconds. So you see where I'm going here. Let's all close our eyes and simply just rest in silence and darkness for 4.9 seconds. Here we go. Congratulations. You just finished your first dark retreat. You know, the idea here is you drip it, you titrate it. So the next step would be 49 seconds. The step after that would be 49 minutes. The next step after that would be 4.9 hours. I mean, again, this is just that playful guide, but the idea, because after 4.9 hours then it becomes somewhat exponential, you know, 4.9 days, 4.9 weeks, so this little model can be released. But I mentioned this, Michael, because by far the best way to get into this is in a titrated, graduated way, where you play with it, become familiar with it. The very definition of the word meditation, by the way, in the Tibetan language, gom, G-O-M, means to become familiar with. So the idea here is to drip the darkness on the terms that make it very workable and negotiable for you. So sometimes, you know, people, 49 minutes, hey, I can do that. I can practice with my eyes closed for 49 minutes, or I can put a mask on or go into the dark. Well, when you start to pass, you know, the couple-hour mark, half-day mark kind of thing, then things become increasingly interesting, revelatory, and restorative. And so from there, then the really the magic really starts, actually begins. And one needs to go cautiously, safely, feeling the pressure when the pressure does arise. I can talk a little bit about why that pressure is there, you know, why is it so difficult up front. Because often, I can speak from my own experience, Michael, when I first started, way, you know, decades ago, this was not easy. I mean, it really was difficult. I did not have enough personal guidance. I went in for a week. I broke it up. I did a day within this week. I set off a cabin for a week. I went in for one day. It was all part of the same week. Then I took an afternoon off and I went in for three days. And then so I gradually expanded, you know, one day, three day, five days, seven days, and then just continued to grow. But if you do it this way, and also what's called a gray retreat, because some people may be interested in this, and they may be like, there's no effing way I'm going to do this. They're just intimidated. Well, if you titrate it this way, or you do a gray retreat, which is my languaging for just weaving in and out of darkness, this practice becomes completely workable, very reasonable. And you can start to tap into the extraordinary capacities, the gifts that this practice actually has to offer. So I'll pause yet again, because there's so many directions we can take it here.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: No, this is super fascinating. I have eager ears. I want to hear more. Let's start talking about, again, the benefits, because that's the place I interrupted you for this question. But starting with the benefits that might happen at 49 minutes, you know, and then kind of expanding out with time, if that's a good way to unpack that.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Yeah. So there are an unusually large number of benefits, almost disproportionate. You know, like I mentioned, the ROI on this practice is crazy. People come out of retreat saying traumas have been healed. You might be surprised, like trauma, people are going into the dark to work with trauma. Yes. Almost miraculous — and sometimes I would say miraculous — levels of physical healing take place. I've heard people coming in like, you know, I've had this headache for decades and it's gone. I've had this back pain for five years and it's gone. Creativity — this is definitely my experience — can absolutely just explode in the darkness, which is why artists, creator types, musicians, poets and whatnot, when they're getting wind of this, they're starting to go in and explore it. Meditative types can come out — and I'm part of this bandwagon — saying this is the most profound, transformative thing I've ever done in my life. And so the level of creativity, insight, healing, restoration is ridiculous. And so why is that, Michael? So this is what I became super interested in, in the survey over my many years of doing this, that when I started talking to all my neuroscience friends, they go, wow, this is really interesting, was developing a model, a map, for where these extraordinary restorative capacities can, how they can take place. But immediately I have to interject, this doesn't also happen to everybody. So this is really important. It's very easy to think, oh my gosh, I just have to do this. This is the next big panacea, the silver bullet. No, no, it's not. On one level, you can say it's just meditation on steroids. Rudy Gobert, the NBA superstar, when he came out, he said something quite nicely. He said, dark retreat is meditation times a thousand. And there's some real insight to that comment. But I'm going to qualify throughout our conversation that there are a number of people that this practice is something that they definitely should not do. Those who suffer from any level of depersonalization, derealization, dissociation disorders like dissociative identity disorder, those types of things, certain psychiatric conditions or others, that are absolutely, positively contraindicated. Most people self-select to this practice. In other words, those who are afflicted with claustrophobia, nyctophobia, fear of the dark, they're just going to go, there's no way I'm going to do this, and say they stay out, which is great. But other people kind of pass the self-select boundary, they go in. And if they don't have the right approach, they can get in trouble, especially when they feel like they have to achieve. They set out, oh, I'm going to do five days, hell or high water. Oh my goodness, don't do that. That's where you can get into trouble. But in terms of like where the restoration and the extraordinary healing capacities come from, the model — there's several here I can explore, but one of the things that's most fantastically revelatory for me, and this ties in also to what's called the meta-crisis, the poly-crisis, you know, this collective shitshow that we're facing in the world today, this could potentially help us address even that. And so the following here to me is quite important. This has been a big discovery for me, that when I go into the dark, I fundamentally can no longer distract in my normal ways, right? Etymologically, this is so interesting. I love word origins. To distract literally means to pull apart. And Laka Rinpoche once said, to end distraction is to end samsara. Well, he doesn't say it, but it's implied: to amp distraction is to amp samsara. And we live in the dark age, the degenerate age, the Kali Yuga, which its signature is runaway, rampant distraction, brought about largely in this day and age by excessive artificial light. Literally, these weapons of mass distraction that we hold in our hands that are always pulling us away from the present moment. So my experience, and this is what we're going to be studying, is that by pulling out all distractions — this is the genius of this meditation, Michael — is it doesn't really add anything. This practice is like the addition of a tool designed for subtraction. Meister Eckhart said it: the soul does not grow by addition but by subtraction. And so when you're in the dark and you can no longer fracture away, break away, dismember, you are almost forced to remember. Like, Plato was onto this, this whole notion of anamnesis, or the path is one of recollection. The essence of psycho-spiritual development really is remembrance. The path is one of remembrance, i.e., sati.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Bingo.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: It's exactly. And so when you go into the dark and you can no longer literally distract in the normal ways, you're forced into the center of your centerless self. You're forced to basically retreat in the best sense. And as you fall into this ground of being — and I can give you in perhaps a minute or two a really interesting tour of my own experience over many years of doing this, this kind of archaeology of consciousness, how the mind actually falls into itself through these layers of the pre-conscious, subconscious, to the unconscious, to the collective unconscious, to the domain of the deities, the gods and the archetypes, and then even further, handed off to the wisdom traditions, the super unconscious, clear light mind, or the reduction base. And so as the mind returns to its natural state of unity, non-duality — so underneath this all, Michael, is the trajectory of non-duality. My languaging: darkness is the color of non-duality. And so as you return to this reduction base and fundamentally remember who you are, a natural consequence of that is incredible healing and restoration. So it's as if — I'm a skier, so let's say I go skiing and I break my leg. I go see my orthopedic surgeon. I have two fractured, you know, bones in my thigh. Well, what does he do? Well, he approximates this fundamental duality. He puts these fractured bones in approximation. And then what does he do? He puts them in a holding cast. And then what happens is the natural restorative agencies of the body-mind go to work to heal. Healing at a physical level is remembrance. Healing at a psychospiritual level is remembrance. So the essence, I'm arguing — it may seem facile, but I think on one level it can be argued that the essence not only of all my issues in life, but the essence of the meta-crisis that we're facing today, is one fracture upon the next, one dismemberment upon the next, one instance of forgetfulness, distraction, upon the next. And so by getting rid of all the opportunities for dismemberment, for fracturing, for distracting, well, guess what happens? Nature takes over. Restoration takes over. Healing. All these amazing things simply take place, not because you've added anything, but you've simply stopped breaking away. This is really important, because even the languaging of the fruitions of the spiritual path intimate this. We talk about non-duality, right? Term of negation. Nirvana, extinction. Nirodha, cessation. Nishprapancha. These are all terms of cessation or negation. So even the languaging of these states of enlightenment are intimations of this process of restoration and reunion and healing. And so again, I'll pause, because I can say a little bit more about my journey, which is not linear, by the way. This is not a linear journey. It's definitely more like a pinball, pinging all over in the dark. But I've noticed over decades of doing it that there does seem to be a particular trajectory here, that even in the wisdom traditions, as I studied this literature — and there's not a lot, but if it's there I read it — they do not talk about these dimensions of Western, so to speak, articulation of the mind. And so what I try to do in my work, in my writing now, is bring the best of the East and the West conjoined with science to support why I think this practice is so transformative. And I'm delighted that the scientists I'm working with are completely in resonance with this and are willing to get behind it. And now we're collecting the data.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So fascinating. So the question that's arising, and this is a lead-in to you talking about your own experience of, let's just say, the mind deconstructing, which is what I'm hearing you talk about or wanting to talk about. My question is, what is the relationship between going into the dark like this and, let's say, the alaya vijnana?

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Okay, wonderful. A little geek speak here. I love it, Michael. So, well, a couple things. So, first of all, we need to understand that the alaya vijnana is the reduction base of samsara. So, for our listeners, let's define some of these terms. This is important. So, the term — let's just stay with vijnana for starters. So, vijnana is composed of two aspects, the word itself. J-N-A-N-A, jnana. Jnana in Sanskrit; in Bengali, jnana, right?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Or, yeah, gyana in Hindi pronunciation.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Exactly. So this word, jnana, translates as, you could say in our language, in kind of non-dual wisdom. You put the prefix vi — this is where it gets really interesting. So jnana would be one of many synonyms for this reduction base that I'm referring to, the bottomless bottom of reality and mind itself. It's one way to language it. Now, this is where it gets really interesting. You put the prefix vi in front of it. Vi in Sanskrit means fractured, bifurcated, divided. So vijnana is one term in Sanskrit for consciousness. So consciousness is actually — this is a subtle but important difference — consciousness is bifurcated, divided, fractured non-dual wisdom. Consciousness is always a pejorative term. It always denotes duality. And so when you're cascading, when the mind falls into itself, the term in Tibetan here is literally rangbop, R-A-N-G-B-O-P, it literally means self-fall. When the mind falls into itself — deep meditation, in deep dreamless sleep, in death, or in dark retreat — it falls through the sedimentation levels of both the conscious and the unconscious mind. This is where it gets incredibly interesting. And so as it bottoms out, as you go through this descent, like I mentioned earlier, from the pre-conscious to the subconscious to the unconscious to the collective unconscious of depth psychology and Jungian work, then you hand the baton over to the wisdom traditions. The bedrock of the relative unconscious mind is the alaya vijnana. Alaya in this case basically just means range, like Himalaya, range of consciousness. And so this is the bedrock of the relative self-sense. So you fall into that, and then eventually, Michael, you fall into and then through that. And then what happens is, well, the vi, which represents division, fracturing, duality, that prefix is taken away, and vijnana then collapses into jnana. Consciousness then collapses and falls into, relaxes into, opens into non-dual wisdom. Now you're talking about the ground, the bedrock of both samsara and nirvana, the irreducible reduction base of the whole shebang. And so, again, other methods can do this. High-dose 5-MeO-DMT can do this. Deep intensive meditation can do this. Sleep yoga, dream yoga can do this. Death, by the way, is going to do this, which is why this practice came about as a preparation for death, so that you could, as so many wisdom traditions say, die before you die. So dark retreat for me — this is why I started doing it, Michael, because as you know, I write and teach a lot about death. I went in there basically to learn how to die. And in fact, I did. And so this is the most incredible journey that arguably, according to especially Tibetan Buddhism and the tradition, is recapitulated, reiterated as we fall into the ultimate dark retreat involuntarily at the end of life, right? So you fall into and through the relative unconscious mind and then into the deep creative clear light mind, or the absolute clear light mind bedrock, which is jnana itself. And so I want to make sure we talk about — I'm going to ping something so that we can circle back into it — about how darkness is itself a duality decimator. This is really, really important. I'm intimating it with this conversation, right, with what I just said. But I want to come back and say a little bit more about this. But I also want to pause, because this is a big deal, how it is that dark retreat heals all these dualities. Remember, darkness is the color of non-duality. But I'm going to pause before I go there, because I just unloaded my mouthful and I want to make sure it's clear.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It is clear. And again, totally interesting. I'm wanting you to come back around to where you said you were going to talk about your own experience of your mind unpacking itself.

transcript.speaker: Andrew Holecek
transcript.text: Yeah. Okay. Yeah. You can see how jazzed I get about this. So yeah. So let me just start at the top.
